articles.subtitle: Apple released the all-new MacBook Neo earlier this year, and it’s been a resounding success by all indications. Here’s everything we know so far about what’s next for Apple’s most affordable laptop … MacBook Neo 2 features A19 Pro chip The current...
articles.author: 9to5Mac
articles.content:
Apple released the all-new MacBook Neo earlier this year, and it’s been a resounding success by all indications. Here’s everything we know so far about what’s next for Apple’s most affordable laptop …

MacBook Neo 2 features

A19 Pro chip

The current MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip, which is the same chip used in the iPhone 16 Pro. As reported by Bloomberg, Apple is working on a next-generation MacBook Neo powered by the A19 Pro chip.

In terms of performance, the A19 Pro is about 10-15% faster than the A18 Pro in single-core and multi-core CPU tests. The jump in GPU performance is even bigger, with benchmarks showing an up to 40% boost for the A19 Pro. This is because every GPU core in the A19 Pro has Neural Accelerators built in.

The A19 Pro chip is also used in the flagship iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone Air.

According to reporter Tim Culpan, Apple will likely use a “binned” version of the A19 Pro chip in the MacBook Neo. While the A19 Pro chip in the iPhone 17 Pro has a 6-core GPU, the MacBook Neo version of the chip will likely have a 5-core GPU.

More memory

One of the compromises of the MacBook Neo is that it has 8GB of RAM. The rest of Apple’s Mac lineup nowadays starts with 16GB of RAM.

The next-generation MacBook Neo won’t jump all the way to 16GB of RAM. Instead, it’s expected to offer 12GB of RAM thanks to the aforementioned A19 Pro.

As I wrote in my review, I don’t think it’s a huge limitation that the MacBook Neo has just 8GB of RAM. Still, an increase for the next-generation model is a great improvement.

New AI features

The combination of the A19 Pro chip and 12GB of RAM upgrades should also unlock support for Apple’s more powerful on-device AI model announced at WWDC. This model enables a more accurate dictation experience and new options for customizing the Siri voice.

The current MacBook Neo doesn’t support this feature because of its A18 Pro chip and 8GB of RAM.

New colors

The MacBook Neo is available in an array of fun colors, including citrus, blush, indigo, and silver. Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plan is to “periodically” update the MacBook Neo with new colors.

There aren’t any details on which colors the next-generation MacBook Neo will be available in.

articles.title: Wild report claims Apple might launch an M5 Ultra MacBook Pro
articles.subtitle: Macworld Reports about Apple switching its MacBooks and iPads to OLED displays have been circulating in the rumor mill for some time now.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Reports about Apple switching its MacBooks and iPads to OLED displays have been circulating in the rumor mill for some time now. A new report by Omdia gives us a more concrete look at when the switch could actually happen, as well as a few far-out details about Apple’s alleged plans.

The first MacBook equipped with an OLED display will reportedly be available “by the end of 2026,” according to the site, which is in line with previous rumors. The MacBook Omdia is referring to is likely to be Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro, which is expected later this year or in early 2027.

It appears, however, that the touchscreen MacBook will be a new addition to the MacBook Pro lineup, a higher-end model that could fall under Apple’s Ultra branding. Omdia states that “the existing 14.3-inch and 16.3-inch MacBook Pro models with LCD + Mini LED backlighting will not be discontinued,” which means the MacBook Pro lineup, as it is now, will continue, with Apple upgrading the chip on a regular basis.

Surprisingly, and perhaps unbelievably, Omdia predicts that this new model is “highly likely to be equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.” Apple’s M5 ultra chip is only used in the Mac Studio, which includes a complex thermal cooling system with a heavy copper heat sink that adds two pounds to the machine’s weight.

Omdia also reports that the MacBook Air will continue to use an LCD display, and that there’s a “new 13.8-inch MacBook, which is expected to launch in 2029 with a hybrid OLED display.” This “new” MacBook is likely an upgraded version of the MacBook Air, which has been reported by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman to be making the switch to OLED in the future.

Omida also confirms previous reports that an OLED iPad mini will arrive later this year. The current LCD iPad mini was released in October 2024, so it’s due for an update. It would be Apple’s first non-Pro tablet to have an OLED display.

articles.title: Rust's New Force Wipe Update Includes Major Game Changes
articles.subtitle: Facepunch wants to make the early game harder for clans It's the first Thursday of September, which means it's the best day of the month for Rust players — force wipe.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Facepunch wants to make the early game harder for clans

It's the first Thursday of September, which means it's the best day of the month for Rust players — force wipe. This force wipe update has been titled "Breach and Clear," as it's all about breaking obstacles and destroying lootable structures. Over a hundred minor updates have been made to improve the overall state of the game, and dozens of major changes have also been applied, many of them in an attempt to balance the game for solo players who have to face zergs and large clans.

Every month, hundreds of players become prim-locked for the first few days of the wipe, as clans take over monuments and grab all available blueprints. They then have to wait for these clans to sell blueprints in their shops to finally get a Tier 2 workbench and start crafting proper weapons. To slow down their progression, Facepunch has added monument blockers to red keycard puzzle rooms.

While some are weaker and can be broken with a melee weapon, others require several jackhammers to destroy. The blockers' upkeep lasts 24 hours, after which they begin to decay. This won't significantly impede progression, but it's bound to make the first day or so a bit more interesting.

Tool Cupboard upkeep cost now increases according to team size

Image: Facepunch

Another thing that groups will have to worry about is increased Tool Cupboard (TC) upkeep based on the number of players in the base. There is no tax for bases with only four players. If there are six players, upkeep increases by 2%, and this number increases by 4% for each additional player. The maximum upkeep tax is 300%.

To determine upkeep tax, the TC counts players authorized on the TC and code locks (including guest codes). It also counts players who have been deauthorized on the TC and code locks in the last 24 hours to prevent teams from bypassing the fee. On the bright side, clan ore farmers should have an easier time managing upkeep, as high quality metal ore nodes and harvestables can now be found and broken for HQM ore.

The Power Trip update that went live in August made it so players had to power up the Power Plant in order to bring electricity to the entire island. To make this feature even more important, electricity across the island is now required for Outpost drones to pick up items from players' shops.

These are the most important features in September's update. However, minor changes and additions have also been made, and some are worth noting. Fans can read the full patch notes in September's devblog. Here are a few changes that stand out:

New Tier 1 healing item, Medical Honey Bandage, heals more than Bandage and less than Medical Syringe. Requires honey to craft.

Attack helicopter armor now detaches as damage is dealt to it.

Heavy Plate Jacket and Pants now make noise when moving. Heavy Plate Helmet suppresses noise.

Certain pie buffs have been increased. Recipes have been tweaked.

Large Medkit now removes radiation

Lastly, Rust 's weekly store has been updated with an array of items. On top of this, the highly anticipated Crystal Assault Rifle DLC has been added to the item store. This beautiful translucent weapon comes in five different colors (diamond, ruby, pink diamond, emerald, and sapphire) and can be purchased on Steam for $6.99.

And the Battle Pass system is no longer on it

articles.title: macOS 27 Golden Gate: New features, release date, beta, compatible Macs
articles.subtitle: Macworld Apple has already revealed many of the new features coming in macOS 27 Golden Gate, the next major update for the Mac.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Apple has already revealed many of the new features coming in macOS 27 Golden Gate, the next major update for the Mac. Headline changes include an all-new Siri AI assistant, major upgrades to apps including Safari, Photos, Messages, Mail and Calendar, expanded child-safety features, design refinements and performance improvements throughout the operating system. We’ve also had the chance to see many of these features in action through the beta, with the full release now likely to be only days away.

Golden Gate continues Apple’s tradition of naming macOS releases after iconic Californian landmarks. More broadly, the update represents another step in Apple’s push to make the Mac smarter and more proactive, with greater use of Apple Intelligence across the operating system and a stronger focus on helping users complete everyday tasks more quickly.

macOS 27 will support all Macs powered by Apple silicon, marking the end of the road for Intel-based Macs. While Intel models won’t be eligible for the new operating system, Apple is expected to continue providing security updates for them for some time.

Apple made developer and public betas of macOS 27 available, with the finished version expected in September 2026. This hub covers everything you need to know about macOS 27 Golden Gate, including its new features, compatibility, beta releases and Apple Intelligence upgrades.

What’s New in macOS 27 Golden Gate at a glance

Apple

Here are the top ten new features and changes coming with macOS 27 Golden Gate.

Siri AI: A redesigned conversational Siri that can answer questions, understand personal and onscreen context, access the web and take actions across apps.

Apple Intelligence: Systemwide proofreading, smarter writing tools, improved dictation and automatic file and folder naming.

Safari upgrades: Automatic tab grouping, webpage change alerts with Notify Me, AI-generated extensions and faster, more efficient browsing.

Smarter Messages and Mail: Personalized Smart Reply, better search and syncing, contextual suggestions and improved reliability.

New Photos tools: Spatial Reframing, image expansion with Extend, improved Clean Up and better search and organisation.

More powerful built-in apps: New features for Passwords, Calendar, Notes, Preview, Freeform, Weather, Shortcuts and Image Playground.

Expanded parental controls: Ask to Browse, improved Screen Time, contact approvals and broader Communication Safety protections.

Better Mac gaming: Game Porting Toolkit 4 promises significant performance and compatibility improvements for Windows games.

Refined Liquid Glass design: Better readability and consistency, adjustable transparency, cleaner Finder windows and improved iPhone Mirroring.

Faster macOS performance: Quicker app launches, Spotlight, AirDrop and networking, plus improved external-display, Thunderbolt and Bluetooth support.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: Mousey city-builder Whiskerwood gets a bit wetter today with a hefty nautical update that lets your rodent kingdom venture out on the open seas
articles.subtitle: Watch out for pirats You like putting a bunch of mice on a boat, don't you? Of course you do, it's always enjoyable seeing semi-anthropomorphic mice do human things!
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
Watch out for pirats

You like putting a bunch of mice on a boat, don't you? Of course you do, it's always enjoyable seeing semi-anthropomorphic mice do human things! Now that we're on the same page, this is a good time to let you know that the new update for Whiskerwood, a city-builder where the cities are filled with mice ruled by nasty, greedy cats, has received a new update today where the friendly rodents can venture out to sail the seven seas.

Appropriately titled the Nautical Update, this one's all about boats, boat battles, ships, shipyards, trading, and more. As explained in a Steam blog post, the devs over at Minakata Dynamics consider this to be the second act of the game, the first act being the inhabitants of your city coming to terms with living under the rule of those aforementioned cats, the Claws. Prior to this update you were just focused on the one little island you inhabited, but now you'll be able to go out and see the world.

"In doing so, you'll encounter Pirates, whose threat slowly wears away at the Claw's colony system," the blog post explains. "These lawless Pirates smuggle and pillage from the Colonies and challenge the Claw's nautical supremacy. Either willingly or by force, your actions will feed the pirates. In turn, the Pirate Wars will bring the Claws to acts of desperation, acts which will grant you the schematics to outfit a navy!"

Getting the map is quite literal, as the whole thing shows you a 2D, grid-based map where you choose where you want your ships to go. Along the way you can take part in battles, or you can fish, and on certain islands you'll be able to trade goods to build up your personal supply of resources. On top of this, "keeping your crew alive is vital, as not just any Whisker can crew a ship.

Only Whiskers with the new skills of Sailor or Officer can set sail. Larger ships require Officers & Sailors, while smaller ships can make do with only Sailors. "

Plus on top of this, your home island can get attacked too, so you need to be prepared to defend it while you're out on your adventures. A fairly hefty sounding update! And the game's 50% off for a little while too, so, can't go wrong really. You can check it out on Steam here.

articles.title: Meta launches Muse Voice Transcribe for real-time voice dictation on Mac
articles.subtitle: Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.

Muse Voice Transcribe powers system-wide dictation on Mac

Meta Superintelligence Labs says Muse Voice Transcribe combines streaming automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization and endpointing.

In practical terms, it can transcribe speech as it happens, separate speakers across recordings with 20-plus voices, and determine when someone has finished talking, all without a separate post-processing step.

The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 validated at launch. It supports audio longer than an hour, plus native code-switching within or between sentences. Language, keyword, and context biasing can further improve recognition.

Rather than using one fixed tradeoff between speed and accuracy, Muse Voice Transcribe decides how long to listen before committing each word. Meta calls this “adaptive delay.” The system can move quickly through easier speech while using more audio context for difficult words.

Meta says the model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis streaming speech-to-text leaderboard as of September 1.

Muse Voice Transcribe is available today through the Meta Model API for $3 per 1,000 audio-minutes, equivalent to $0.18 per hour.

It is also already powering dictation in Meta AI for Mac and Muse Code. On Mac, users can hold the Fn key to dictate into any application.

articles.title: Magic: The Gathering Isn’t Done With Final Fantasy Just Yet
articles.subtitle: Final Fantasy promo cards are officially a trend for Magic Magic: The Gathering ’s most successful Universes Beyond crossover set ever, Final Fantasy, may have been released more than a year ago, but Wizards of the Coast and Square Enix apparently aren’t...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Final Fantasy promo cards are officially a trend for Magic

Magic: The Gathering ’s most successful Universes Beyond crossover set ever, Final Fantasy, may have been released more than a year ago, but Wizards of the Coast and Square Enix apparently aren’t ready to put it to bed just yet. A newly announced promo card keeps the collaboration alive well into 2027.

Thursday morning’s Sony State of Play included an extended gameplay trailer for Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, the final chapter in Square Enix’s FF7 remake trilogy. The publisher announced that the game will be released April 8, 2027, for Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X. Square Enix also revealed preorder information, including an unexpected bonus for Magic fans:

Special day-one physical editions available through participating retailers will include a foil FF7 -themed Magic promo card depicting Cloud Strife clashing with Sephiroth. The card will be available while supplies last, according to Square Enix’s announcement.

Final Fantasy 7's new Magic Promo Card

The card itself is a reprint of Final Showdown, a versatile white instant originally printed as a mythic rare in 2024’s Outlaws of Thunder Junction. Its spree mechanic lets players pay for any combination of three effects: stripping every creature of its abilities for the turn, granting one creature indestructible, or destroying every creature on the battlefield.

That makes Final Showdown an unusually flexible board wipe. At its cheapest, it can protect a crucial creature for two mana. For six mana, it can destroy every creature at instant speed. Paying eight mana activates all three modes in sequence, removing potentially troublesome abilities before making one creature indestructible and destroying everything else. It's a fitting representation of a video game where a giant meteor looms in the sky, threatening to destroy the entire planet.

The original Final Showdown depicts a lone gunslinger walking past a row of bodies on the ground, but the Final Fantasy reprint features new art by Square Enix character designer Tetsuya Nomura depicting Sephiroth and Cloud facing off. Based on the original FF7 canon, however, this cannot be the actual final showdown between the two because Sephiroth has his shirt on. Although, FF7 Remake did break fate itself, so all bets are off.

This also isn’t the first time Square Enix has used a Magic card to sweeten the deal on video game preorders. Physical Nintendo Switch 2 copies of Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth, released in June, included a full-art foil Zack Fair promo featuring artwork by Nomura. In addition to these two promos, Wizards also released other products well after the initial June 2025 launch.

In December 2025, Wizards of the Coast released four Scene Boxes recreating moments from Final Fantasy, Final Fantasy 8, Final Fantasy 9, and Final Fantasy 15. That holiday wave also included a Chocobo Bundle loaded with themed lands and alternate-art cards.

By the time FF7 Revelation comes out, it will have been almost two full years since Final Fantasy cards were first released — is it at all possible we'll get even more FF cards?

For the sake of Hydaelyn, try this Commander out

When Polygon spoke with Magic principal designer Gavin Verhey at MagicCon: Las Vegas in May, he acknowledged that even the massive original set could not cover everything from the franchise’s history.

“We could have made a 2,000-card set and still not covered all the things players wanted to see,” Verhey said. “The set is already huge.”

Verhey explained that the team approached the project as though it might be its only opportunity to adapt Final Fantasy, prioritizing the biggest characters and moments while also making room for deeper cuts. Even so, he was enthusiastic about the possibility of returning to the franchise.

“If we ever got the opportunity to do more, of course, I would leap at the opportunity,” Verhey said. “There’s a lot of other cool stuff to do there. We did not touch any of the side games. We could always tap into those.”

Another Final Fantasy set is far from confirmed. But between the December product wave, the Zack Fair promo, and now Final Showdown, supplemental releases are starting to look like a pattern — and with Final Fantasy 7 Revelation still seven months away, there is plenty of time for Magic ’s most successful crossover to deliver another big surprise.

articles.title: ‘Worst Crash We’ve Seen Since the 1980s,’ Warns Epic Games CEO
articles.subtitle: Epic’s Tim Sweeney and other industry experts don't have good things to say about how AAA games are doing The video game industry has seen better days.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Epic’s Tim Sweeney and other industry experts don't have good things to say about how AAA games are doing

The video game industry has seen better days. Between a nonstop wave of layoffs over the last few years and a w orsening hardware crisis that is flatlining console sales, things are a bit bleak at the moment. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney described the situation as the biggest crash the industry has seen since the infamous 1980s recession. For context, that crash saw game console revenue drop by 97% from 1983 to 1985.

Hardware component shortages are a big factor

As per GameIndustry.biz, Edge magazine’s Alex Spencer spoke with nine experts for issue 428, asking whether the current situation can be described as a “Crash 2.0.” Sweeney described the ongoing hardware component shortage as a key reason things are so bad right now. He said the following:

There’s an unprecedented wave of investment in building AI systems and data centres, based on the belief that they’re going to have a really transformational role in the economy, and the scale of the economic opportunity there means they can outbid the entire entertainment industry for all the components.

So we’re getting the short end of the stick, and the prices of RAM and storage are quadrupling, and not necessarily stopping there. We should expect there’s just going to be a continual supply crisis for all gaming-relevant hardware for the next three years. The only solution, I think, is going to be building massive new factories to meet the world’s capacity demands – and that will happen.

So we’re getting the short end of the stick, and the prices of RAM and storage are quadrupling, and not necessarily stopping there.

We should expect there’s just going to be a continual supply crisis for all gaming-relevant hardware for the next three years. The only solution, I think, is going to be building massive new factories to meet the world’s capacity demands – and that will happen.

Video game console sales have been down across the board, with July proving the lowest month for gaming hardware spending since the COVID-19 pandemic caused supply chain shortages. Prices for the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and Nintendo Switch 2 have gone up due to RAM shortages.

AAA game budgets have ballooned in recent years

Sweeney added that there are also “internal dysfunctions” that are contributing to the industry’s woes, such as the ballooning cost of AAA game development. Playable Worlds CEO Raph Koster argued the same. “I think the first time I spoke about, ‘Hey, cost is going to kill us’ was in 2005,” he said. He previously said the cost of AAA game development goes up about tenfold each decade.

According to his analysis, when adjusted for inflation, it cost around $1 million to make a big-budget game in the mid ‘90s, $10 million in 2005, and $100 million in 2015.

While that rate has slowed down a bit, with Sweeney saying higher-end games cost between $250 million and $400 million, these budgets are arguably unsustainable because financial resources are “the great constraint that never gets expanded,” as former PlayStation boss Shawn Layden put it. He argues that games need to shrink in scope. “Do you need to model an entire world that takes 45 minutes to walk across?

If there’s not a reason for that – if it’s not pushing the experience or story forward – that’s just a party trick. You’ve spent a bunch of time – which means money – on something that doesn’t mean anything. ”

Both Koster and former Tencent business development director Amir Satvat argued that AI won’t solve these problems. “AI is not a platform reset, where costs get lower. AI is just a computer getting bigger, and so the gas will keep filling it,” Koster said. “It is actually incredibly expensive, in the end, so most of the benefit flows upwards. AI is changing things very rapidly, and it also doesn’t matter.”

“Are you actually getting a measurable productive gain in what you’re doing because you’re using these tools? ” Satvat added. “I’ve seen firms that made staff reductions because they thought they could, due to AI, and are now realising that they cut too many people and are hiring back.

” Satvat put the massive cuts to the game industry in perspective, saying, “I think this is as bad as the ’83 crash if you’re a game developer based in North America or Western Europe, in a traditional AAA studio. That is ground zero for destruction. ”

In July, Xbox announced that it was laying off 3,200 employees over the next quarter while cutting ties with four of its studios. Although Star Wars: Zero Company launched to widespread acclaim and performed well on Steam’s charts, it was revealed a few days ago that the game’s developer, Bit Reactor, had furloughed up to 80% of its staff. Stories like that have unfortunately become the norm.

articles.title: Perplexity Introduces ‘Hybrid Compute’ for Computer Agent on Apple Silicon Macs
articles.subtitle: Source: Perplexity. Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based. Recently, Perplexity also introduced Portable Computer, a local-first version of Computer that can escalate work to the cloud with a user’s permission.

Hybrid compute approaches the problem from a different direction. Tasks start in the cloud but if a new local classifier detects potentially sensitive information, the user is alerted and asked whether they want to route it to a local model, although users also have the option to let the flagged data be used by a frontier cloud-based model. Gemma E4B, Qwen3.6 35B-A3B, and a Perplexity post-trained version of Qwen3.6 35B are available at launch for that local work, with more models to come in the future.

Tasks that don’t require sensitive information are handled in the cloud by frontier models that also orchestrate the cloud and local tasks. Users select the cloud orchestrator and Perplexity chooses the helper frontier models used.

Another key feature is that hybrid compute works with tasks begun from an iPhone or iPad, too. Those devices could already kick off a session, but now they can also run tasks that use sensitive information locally if your Mac is turned on and running Perplexity.

Yesterday, I got a demo of the feature that walked through three scenarios:

an attorney researching a legal brief, with sensitive client data on their Mac, allowing them to update it locally,

an analyst using web-based data to update a confidential slide deck for a presentation about a company’s financials, and

a small business owner kicking off pricing research from her iPhone that was combined with private pricing data for her business that never left her Mac.

I haven’t tried hybrid compute myself yet, but if it works as advertised, it’s a big step forward for Perplexity, and one that a lot of its competitors are also chasing. AI agents are only as good as the tools and data to which they have access.

Tool calling has been a big focus over the last year and more, but data privacy is an equally important issue that needs to be solved before more companies, especially those in regulated industries, adopt agentic tools like Personal Computer. It’s good to see Perplexity tackling this head-on.

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: Switch Online Just Got One of Nintendo's Greatest Racing Games of All Time
articles.subtitle: Rarely matched and never bested on its platform As it often does, Nintendo just released a new batch of games that are available to play on its Switch Online service. They come from a variety of genres, but they’re all NES classics of varying renown.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Rarely matched and never bested on its platform

As it often does, Nintendo just released a new batch of games that are available to play on its Switch Online service. They come from a variety of genres, but they’re all NES classics of varying renown. Launch the app on your Nintendo Switch or Switch 2 to enjoy Ninja Gaiden 3: The Ancient Ship of Doom, Ikari Warriors, or the excellent R.C. Pro-Am 2.

Of the lot, R. C. Pro-Am 2 is secretly the best pick for a good time. The Ikari Warriors series (which was part of the SNK Anniversary Collection a few years back) started in arcades and provided a middling experience on console hardware, with the first installment arguably being the least interesting.

Ninja Gaiden 3 is the challenging final entry in the original trilogy, but a lot of retro gamers consider the second entry (which was already in the Switch Online library) the best one. That leaves R. C. Pro-Am 2 with the crown, almost by default. It doesn’t hurt that it’s also a really good game.

Developed by Rare, which is best known these days for the likes of Sea of Thieves and Banjo-Kazooie, R.C. Pro-Am 2 took virtually everything that was great about its predecessor and improved upon it. Nintendo published the first entry, which was a fun little racer despite some big issues: there’s not much variety in venues, vehicle upgrades are minimal, the AI sometimes feels a bit cheap (even when you rely on explosives to even the score), and only one person can play.

Tradewest published the sequel, which addressed every one of those shortcomings. On the original NES hardware, R.C. Pro-Am 2 was one of several games that supported the multitap accessory to extend the number of players to four. Most of us didn’t have the luxury of testing that feature at the time, and we’re unlikely to have much luck gathering like-minded friends to enjoy a little friendly competition in 2026. There’s always online play, though.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Free. Unsubscribe anytime.

R. C. Pro-Am 2 also features three distinct environments: grassland, city, and desert. The first of those, available during the earliest races, closely resembles the tracks in the original R. C. Pro-Am. There are some embellishments, however. Tire piles line tight corners. Streams of water trickle across the course in places, slowing vehicles.

And there are hills to ascend and descend along the way, preventing the experience from feeling flat and barren. The city presents split routes in some areas, with the view of the track occasionally obscured by overpasses. Finally, the desert introduces rough terrain to go along with more frequent passes from overhead planes that pepper the track with bullets.

In the original R. C. Pro-Am, players collected letters to upgrade their remote-controlled vehicles, which is still the case. Part upgrades were mostly found lying on the track, and easy to miss until a person memorized course designs. In the sequel, players collect money bags instead. They then spend their loot in a virtual shop between races.

Upgrades fall into the same general categories: engines, tires, and weapons, mostly. However, there’s more variety. It’s fun to have control over the modifications you make. Decisions about whether to invest in better missiles or save up for that next engine can have long-term impact.

Image: Rare/Tradewest

R.C. Pro-Am 2 is difficult, much like its predecessor, but it also feels more balanced. With sufficient effort, a player should be able to see all the original courses and reach a definitive end to the game. It’s possible to purchase extra continues along the way, in case a race or two goes badly.

Finally, the game also offers occasional multi-player competitions to break up the routine, including a tug-of-war event and a drag race. You’ll play through each of those multiple times during your race through the 32 courses. They’re a welcome opportunity to gain additional resources to spend on upgrades, provided your fingers are fast enough.

R. C. Pro-Am 2 is remembered fondly by the audience it found back in the day, but it released late enough in the NES life cycle that a lot of players overlooked it as they focused on Super Nintendo releases. Until it joined the Nintendo Switch Online catalog, the best way to play the game was as part of the Rare Replay collection on Xbox One.

Physical collectors have made the original NES cartridge a fairly expensive acquisition, and reproductions from Strictly Limited Games were made available in limited quantities that might easily fetch three figures. Give it a try on your Switch or Switch 2 and see what the fuss is all about.

articles.title: Apple’s loaded September kicks off with ‘huge launch’ next week
articles.subtitle: Macworld September is always the biggest month of the year for Apple fans. That’s when we get the new operating systems first announced at WWDC in June, new iPhones, new Apple Watches, and sometimes more. This year is especially monumental.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
September is always the biggest month of the year for Apple fans. That’s when we get the new operating systems first announced at WWDC in June, new iPhones, new Apple Watches, and sometimes more.

This year is especially monumental. It’s the first month and the first event helmed by new CEO John Ternus, the release of the biggest OS updates in years with an all-new Siri, and the unveiling of Apple’s first folding iPhone. All that and more are coming this September. Here’s what’s on the way.

New CEO, new iPhone, and more

As of September 1, Tim Cook is out as CEO (taking a backseat role as Chairman) and new CEO John Ternus is at the helm. That means the big Apple event on September 9 will be the first not headlined by Cook in 15 years. In his welcome letter to employees, he promised a “huge launch that’s going to be phenomenal.

” With Ternus at the helm, will the Surprise and Shine event be different in tone or structure from what we’ve seen the last few years? We’ll find out on September 9 at 10 am. Here’s what we expect at the event:

iPhone Ultra: The marquee product of the new lineup will be Apple’s first foldable device, likely to be called iPhone Ultra. We already have a good idea of its design, but we don’t yet know about its features, particularly what Apple is doing with the software. We expect the price to top $2,000.

iPhone 18 Pro/Max: The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will be an evolutionary upgrade from the iPhone 17 Pro. The big updates are a faster A20 Pro processor and a new main camera with variable aperture.

Apple Watch Series 12: We don’t expect much to be new about the Apple Watch Series 12. There should be a faster processor, and Apple is said to be bringing back the ceramic case option, but the rumors say not to expect a change to the design or major new features this year.

Apple Watch Ultra 4: Just like the Series 12, the new Ultra is going to be primarily a “chip and ship” update with no major design changes or new features.

Apple’s iPhone event will be loaded with shiny new products—and hopefully some surprises.

Apple

AirPods 5: Apparently, there’s an AirPods 5 that could ship as early as September. Like AirPods 4, it would come in both standard and active noise-cancelling versions, but we’re not sure what will actually be new. This is not expected to be the AirPods with cameras in them, and it’s unknown what the new features might be.

Apple TV 4K: A new-generation Apple TV box with a new processor that supports the new Siri AI is supposed to ship before the end of the year. It could be announced at the September event, or it could just go up on the website one day. There’s plenty of time for this update to be released in later months, too.

HomePod mini: Just like the new Apple TV box, the main reason for this to exist is to get a new chip that supports Siri AI. As with the Apple TV, this may not even get mentioned at the event at all and could just go up on the website as an update anytime this year.

Smart home hub: The biggest question mark for Apple’s upcoming event is whether or not the company will unveil its new home hub device. This is said to be a tablet-like pad, with a new 7-inch squarish shape, that will come in both base/speaker-mounted or wall-mounted varieties. It will run a new operating system that blends some of the features of Apple Watch and Apple TV.

It’s meant to control your smart home stuff, make FaceTime calls, listen to music, and so on. Rumors say it could launch this fall, but that doesn’t necessarily mean September.

Mac mini and Mac Studio: While announced in August, the new M6 / M5 Pro Mac mini and M5 Max/Ultra Mac Studio are actually shipping starting on September 22.

articles.title: Microsoft announces cap on Xbox Cloud Gaming hours for Game Pass subscribers, admits most aren't using it much anyway
articles.subtitle: Gotta find revenue wherever you can, I guess.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
As Microsoft continues to flail for a remedy to the reputational damage it's incurred as a result of its repeated mass layoffs, bungled industry consolidation strategies, and partnership with Israeli surveillance agencies, its gaming division is returning to a favorite page from its playbook in recent years: Hiking service costs.

Today, Xbox announced that it will implement a monthly cap on Xbox Cloud Gaming hours for Game Pass subscribers. Previously, eligible Game Pass users could use the game streaming service without a time limit; Beginning in November, however, they'll need to purchase additional cloud playtime through the Xbox Store once they expend their allotted cloud gaming hours.

The Cloud Gaming hourly limits will be determined by Game Pass subscription tier:

Game Pass Ultimate: 15 hours

Game Pass Premium: 10 hours

Game Pass Essential: 5 hours

Xbox acknowledged that the rollout of a monthly time limit on cloud gaming hours is "a meaningful change, particularly for players who regularly spend more time gaming through the cloud." But the company offered an estimate of the policy change's impact that suggests most Game Pass subscribers already aren't using cloud gaming much.

"We expect this upcoming change to impact 4% of Game Pass subscribers," Xbox said.

While it'll be rolling out the monthly cloud gaming cap for Game Pass subscribers, Microsoft will also be opening the service for players without Game Pass in November. Any users will be able to stream eligible games to supported devices after purchasing cloud gaming playtime through the Xbox Store.

Xbox didn't confirm how much cloud playtime will cost, but said it will provide "more information about pricing, purchasing additional hours, eligible games, market availability, and how players can check their remaining time" in November.

The changes to cloud gaming access, Xbox says, are a cost saving measure.

"We’re introducing this model because the cost of providing cloud gaming grows as more people use it and play for longer," Xbox said. "Moving to monthly limits allows us to keep offering the service while continuing to invest in its reliability and performance. We understand that for some players the practical result is a higher cost."

Evidently, the company doesn't expect the ad-supported game streaming it began testing last month will sufficiently move the needle on that front. And that needle's got a lot of moving to do: In July, Microsoft's annual financial filings confirmed that Xbox revenue had fallen by $1.7 billion over the last year.

Whether "the practical result" of a higher cost on cloud streaming will actually deliver needed revenue gains for Xbox, however, is unclear. In June, new Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball said the company lost "millions" of Game Pass subscribers after the service's 2025 price hike.

In the meantime, Xbox says it will "listen closely to player feedback before and after the change takes effect and share any adjustments we make."

articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple last week announced two new Mac Studio models, with one built around the M5 Max chip and one around the all-new M5 Ultra chip, replacing the M4 Max and M3 Ultra models that had been on sale since March 2025.

The gap between the two is unusually wide this time. ‌Mac Studio‌ with M5 Max starts at $2,499, holding the price Apple set when it raised Mac prices in June, while ‌Mac Studio‌ with M5 Ultra starts at $5,499, a further $200 increase on the post-June M3 Ultra price and $1,500 above what the M3 Ultra cost at launch.

That makes the premium $3,000 before any configure-to-order options, and memory and storage upgrades are more expensive than usual because of the memory chip shortage. Our guide helps to answer the question of how to decide which of these two ‌Mac Studio‌ models is best for you. The shared features include:

An identical enclosure measuring 3.7 inches tall and 7.7 inches wide

Neural Accelerators built into every GPU core, and hardware-accelerated ray tracing

Hardware-accelerated H.264, HEVC, ProRes, and ProRes RAW, plus AV1 decode

A next-generation SSD architecture that Apple says is up to twice as fast as before

Thunderbolt 5 with up to 120Gb/s of bandwidth, and clustering of multiple systems using RDMA (remote direct memory access)

10Gb Ethernet, HDMI, and an SDXC card slot (UHS-II)

Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 via the N1 chip, both new to the ‌Mac Studio‌

Genlock over USB-C for synchronization with professional camera capture

A 3.5mm headphone jack with support for high-impedance headphones

macOS 27, Apple Intelligence, and Siri AI

Here is everything that differs between the two models:

For the overwhelming majority of buyers, including most professionals, the M5 Max is the more appropriate choice. An 18-core CPU, up to 40 GPU cores with Neural Accelerators, up to 128GB of unified memory, and up to 614GB/s of bandwidth cover workflows such as multi-stream 4K and 6K editing, large Logic sessions with real-time plugins, compiling substantial codebases, and most 3D and motion work.

Apple's own figures support this, with up to 3x faster Magic Mask performance in Blackmagic Design DaVinci Resolve Studio and 1.4x faster scene rendering in Maxon Redshift compared to M4 Max, and graphics that are up to 50% faster than the previous generation. Since memory cannot be added later, the sensible approach is to spend more on unified memory at the point of purchase rather than on the higher chip tier.

You should only choose the M5 Ultra if you anticipate running into a performance ceiling the M5 Max cannot clear. The most obvious use-case is local AI inference, where the whole model needs to be resident in memory. 256GB and 512GB configurations paired with 1.2TB/s of bandwidth allow models with hundreds of billions of parameters to run on the machine itself, which keeps sensitive material on-device and eliminates the recurring cost of paying for cloud inference.

The other workflows that can take advantage of the M5 Ultra include studios finishing 8K material from several cameras at once, where the doubled Media Engine and its four encode engines earn their keep, research and simulation work that needs an enormous memory pool, and anyone who specifically needs six Thunderbolt 5 ports or more than five displays.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: DLSS 5 can be jammed into almost any game now, so I've been playing FM26 with neural rendered little computer people because that's just what I do
articles.subtitle: And here's how I did it.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Ever since the Control mod appeared I've been enjoying jamming the released DLSS 5.dll files into a bunch of different games, to greater or lesser effect. Some games it works well in, some it doesn't quite take and you end up with visuals that look a lot like the characters have worms writhing around under their skin.

Though, I have to say when I stuck it into the review version of The Blood of Dawnwalker and it failed to hook the DLSS pipeline that look kinda worked for my semi-Vrakhiri. Bit of extra undead chic with the game failing to run the DLSS neural rendering feature with actual motion vectors or scene depth.

With the necessary files being released in the early access version of NBA 2K27, they've now been unleashed across the internet and modders have been busy getting game-agnostic versions ready for people to squeeze into any title they fancy. And while the first iteration was focused on Control and then games running DLSS already, there have been mods released—particularly the RenoDX and specifically the ShortFuse mods—which allow you to experiment with pushing DLSS 5 into practically any game you like.

And it's surprisingly easy to do, though not without its awkwardness, too. Well, such is the way with unreleased features shoehorned into games they're not meant to be in, but also such is the way with PC gaming.

The thing that has stood out to me—and something that Andy first noted in his hands-on look at the official technology at Gamescom —is that DLSS 5 really can produce some outstanding visual effects… if used sparingly.

Pick the right model of the three (for me, that's Model C) and drop the intensity of the effect down to around 60 - 70% and you end up with scenes and character models that look better than the originals, but without the over-saturated, overblown very AI look of it dialed up to 11, nor without it looking like it's grinding away or adding its own geometry.

But it's also clear it's one hell of a resource hog. Nvidia has been very clear about this from its recent presentations at Gamescom and a briefing I had at the end of last week; DLSS 5 represents about a 50 - 60% drop in frame rate regardless of the game. Though, sometimes we've seen that performance hit be even greater, especially at 4K.

Running the Control mod on an RTX 5090 I was seeing DLSS Balanced 4K Ultra Ray Tracing running at around 110 fps in standard mode, which then dropped to under 50 fps as soon as DLSS 5 was brought to bear on the game, which is about where Nvidia is pitching the performance hit.

That, in all honesty, is to be expected. When Nvidia first showed off the tech around GDC it was running on a pair of RTX 5090s, so the fact that it can be run at all on single lower-spec GPUs is impressive. But it was also going to be punitive for current generation hardware, which only have tensor cores enough for standard DLSS upscaling.

DLSS 5 in FM26

Okay, it's not photorealism, but I think it looks better.

What I wasn't expecting, though, was to be able to stick DLSS 5 into any game, regardless of whether it had DLSS in there in the first place. Which meant that I, with my 33 year Football Manager addiction, had to see what it does to FM26.

And, well, I'm going to be leaving it enabled. It's not that it suddenly makes the game look photorealistic—as Nvidia itself has said, you need a really good input source to get a really good output from DLSS 5—but on its own it adds in a bunch of things that you otherwise have to mod in yourself from a bunch of other places. And because it's just added in last, and FM isn't hugely demanding, I'm still happily locked to 60 fps anyways.

Those little computer people don't need a whole lot of processing.

But it does improve the environmental lighting of the matches. It makes the pitches look better, there's a tiny amount more detail on the tiny people, on the pitch and in the crowd, and it adds in some improved shadows. But it's not just in the 3D engine, because it also works its neural rendering magic on the player profile pics, too. Which is especially helpful for making the regenerated players look less like plastic Action Man figures (or GI Joes, for my American cousins).

DLSS 5 in FM26

You're getting better regen faces without copy/paste mods.

Normally you'd have to use a mod to get more realistic player faces, and even then they're still just a bunch of AI generated profile pics which get disseminated among the database so you still get identical twins from different parts of the game world. With DLSS 5 I'm just getting a little extra facial detail and realism for my new potato-faced folk.

articles.title: Apple Apparently Cancels Plans for Two New MacBooks
articles.subtitle: Apple has canceled plans for a foldable MacBook and a larger OLED MacBook Pro model, according to research firm Omdia. In a new research note, Omdia said Apple has scrapped development of a large foldable MacBook that would have measured between 16.1 and 18...
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple has canceled plans for a foldable MacBook and a larger OLED MacBook Pro model, according to research firm Omdia.

In a new research note, Omdia said Apple has scrapped development of a large foldable MacBook that would have measured between 16.1 and 18 inches when unfolded. It was previously reported that this device had already slipped out of its original 2026 production window, with Omdia among the firms tracking it at the time, though under that earlier reporting it was generally described as a large-screened foldable iPad rather than a MacBook.

Apple has also apparently called off a separate, previously planned MacBook with an ‌OLED‌ display between 14.4 and 16.1 inches in size, which would have sat in its own tier between the standard ‌MacBook Pro‌ sizes and the canceled foldable. With both of those product lines scrapped, the 14.3 to 16.3 inch size range will seemingly remain exclusive to the ‌MacBook Pro‌ series going forward.

Omdia said Apple's broader strategy of bringing ‌OLED‌ displays to its entire ‌iPad‌ and MacBook lineup has not changed, but the company has reworked which products will get ‌OLED‌ and what specific ‌OLED‌ technology each one uses, a shift that lines up with the changes detailed in Apple's rumored 2026 and 2027 product roadmap.

As part of that same reshuffle, Apple is said to be adding a new 13. 8 inch MacBook positioned between the LCD MacBook Air and the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌, using a new generation of ‌OLED‌ technology that includes an LTPO+ backplane, under-panel camera, and color-filter-on-encapsulation technology, among other features. That new 13.

8 inch model appears to fill the gap in Apple's lineup that the now canceled 14. 4 to 16. 1 inch MacBook ‌OLED‌ would have occupied, positioned below the Pro rather than above it.

The 14.3- and 16.3-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌ ‌OLED‌ models, also referred to as the " MacBook Ultra," are expected to be announced in the second half of 2026 or early 2027. Omdia added that Apple will not discontinue the existing mini-LED ‌MacBook Pro‌ models in those sizes when the high-end ‌OLED‌ versions arrive, and the two display types are expected to sell in parallel for several years, with the mini-LED version likely continuing until at least 2028.

Should you buy a Mac mini now?

articles.title: The Potential of M6 and M5 Ultra for Local AI on macOS
articles.subtitle: Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio. You can read more details about the announcement and related specs in John’s overview.

As someone who’s been working with an M3 Ultra Mac Studio (on loan from Apple) with 512 GB of RAM for the past year (plus two separate M4 Mac minis) with a particular focus on local AI models and performance gains enabled by Apple’s MLX framework, I obviously am very interested in these new machines.

To give you some context: my current workspace for my upcoming iOS and iPadOS 27 review, which lives in Notion, is entirely managed by a series of local agents running the latest DeepSeek-V4-Flash via MLX on the Mac Studio, which continuously scan the project for new notes, sources, and research material that is automatically categorized and linked in the chapters that I’m writing.

So, yes, I’m sure I’ll have more thoughts on the new Mac minis and Mac Studios soon. In the meantime, I thought it’d be fun to break down the local AI-related details from Apple.

First, the M6. While it may not be the powerhouse that the M5 Ultra is, it’s an interesting new chip because of its new 2 nm process and dual Neural Engine system:

M6 is built using cutting-edge 2 nm process technology, packing greater transistor density into a smaller die for a major leap in performance and power efficiency. M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

But that’s not all: the new 12-core GPU (which has two more cores than the M4’s old GPU) now features Neural Accelerators in each core for the first time on the Mac mini. The result, according to Apple, is “4x faster AI performance and 2x faster graphics than Mac mini with M4”. If these numbers hold up and scale linearly, a local Mixture-of-Experts model such as Qwen 3.

5-35B-A3B, which would run at ~17 tokens/sec on average on a base M4 Mac mini with 16 GB of RAM, could realistically generate output at over 60 tokens/second with the base model M6 Mac mini.

Based on what we’ve seen so far, the one downside of the M6 Mac mini is that it does not have Thunderbolt 5 ports; those are exclusive to the M5 Pro model, also announced today. As Apple also notes, Thunderbolt 5 allows multiple M5 Pro Mac minis to run local AI models as a single cluster (for example, using something like exo ).

Alas, that won’t be possible with the M6 Mac mini and its Thunderbolt 4 bandwidth bottleneck. Nonetheless, I’d be intrigued to compare the performance of the widely regarded Qwen3. 8-27B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash models on the new M6 Mac mini.

Moving on to the flagship M5 Ultra Mac Studio, let’s start here:

With M5 Ultra, Mac Studio achieves up to 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of M3 Ultra and a staggering 9.8x more than M1 Ultra. Combined with up to 512GB of unified memory and 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth, 50 percent higher than before, Mac Studio lets users run massive models entirely on device with complete privacy — without counting tokens or worrying about rising cloud costs.

As seen on the Mac Studio’s product page, the 512 GB RAM version of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio will only be available in “late October”. Unlike the M6, the M5 Ultra supports Thunderbolt 5, which will allow customers to run multiple Mac Studios in a cluster with shared memory to distribute inference across machines. And, according to Apple, a cluster of four Mac Studios yields three times the performance of a single Mac Studio.

Speaking from personal experience, I know that my M3 Ultra Mac Studio using oMLX can run DeepSeek-V4-Flash locally with generation averaging 35 tokens/second. Assuming a linear 4x increase, that would put the same model at over 120 tokens/second on an M5 Ultra Mac Studio.

To put things in perspective, that kind of performance would be faster than any AI chatbot website, it’d be faster than many providers who offer a “fast” mode for their models, and it’d only be second to either dedicated NVIDIA PC clusters at home or specialized inference providers such as Cerebras or Groq …which are running in full-blown data centers.

Sure, you would need a computer that is likely going to cost more than $20,000 to make it happen, but it’d still be possible on a single machine that is small, quiet, and that – in theory – any consumer can buy off the shelf.

It’s also interesting to consider the implications of M5 Ultra for running much larger models that would have typically required aggressive quantization to even stay in memory and produce any useful output. For example, Z. ai’s GLM-5.

2 (a 744B MoE model) could run at up to 17 tokens/second on an M3 Ultra Mac Studio with 512 GB of RAM; the same person was even able to get the massive Kimi K3 model to run on a single machine…with decoding performance up to 3 tokens/second.

articles.title: Owner of nearly decade-old Dell laptop reportedly wore through the wrist rest and is 'being stabbed by carbon fibers'
articles.subtitle: Ouch.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Every time I use my laptop I get that pins and needles feeling in my hands. It’s like a cactus constantly pricking me. Turns out it’s this Dell XPS 9370 I’ve worn through the palm rests, and now I’m just being stabbed by carbon fibers. In hindsight, it is perhaps a bad… pic.twitter.com/cA30b2Tr1A September 1, 2026

A user on X reported feeling pins and needles in their hands whenever they used their Dell XPS 9370 laptop. After investigation, it turns out, "I’ve worn through the palm rests, and now I’m just being stabbed by carbon fibers." Ouch.

That's according to user X user Parker Drouillard (via International Cyber Digest ), who compares the feeling to being constantly hurt by a cactus. They tag Dell and say: "In hindsight, it is perhaps a bad design. How is this not a health hazard?"

Notably, the XSP 13 (from around 2018) black and white model appears to have a carbon fiber composite palm rest, which is the part that has been worn down from use. They have since put their finger under a microscope, showing off the flecks of what is reportedly carbon fiber embedded in their skin. The user also reports " severe issues " with their contact lenses and says it is "most probably irritation" from the carbon fiber. Again, ouch.

There is one peculiarity here, in that the video of the microscope has a 2019 time stamp on the bottom. Reverse image searching Drouillard's photos suggests they are original, so this might simply be a problem with the camera or microscope.

Carbon fiber is a dangerous material to work with when it splinters like this. It can further shatter or break when embedded in your skin, making it hard to remove; some types of carbon fiber have toxic coatings, and getting anything embedded in your skin makes you more susceptible to infections and rashes. And that's before mentioning the problems with ingesting carbon fiber, which you very easily could do if it sticks to your fingers.

This is how it looks under my microscope. pic.twitter.com/IaHnt5TlPr September 2, 2026

For now, Drouillard has simply taped over the palm rests, though their comment section suggests using epoxy, urethane, or simply a " bunch of different stickers ".

Carbon fiber is a fairly common building material for PC hardware. We've seen a Corsair mouse, a Keychron keyboard concept, an Asus mouse, and even an HP laptop made out of the stuff. This choice of material makes sense, so long as it is adequately treated; carbon fiber is very tough but also very light, which means an uber-lightweight mouse doesn't have to feel flimsy because of the material choice.

There are measures that companies can, and likely do, take against traditional wear and tear when using a material like carbon fiber.

Dell has yet to respond to this complaint, and we don't know exactly how the laptop has been treated in the last decade, but it's definitely made me more cautious about the long-term effects of carbon fiber gear—especially if you like to hang onto your hardware for a long time.

articles.title: Mini-LED MacBook Pro Models Could Stick Around Until 2028

articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple has reportedly revised its plans for adopting OLED displays across its MacBook lineup, and its existing LCD-based MacBook Pro models with mini-LED backlighting are now expected to remain available for longer than anticipated.

According to a new OLED adoption roadmap published by research firm Omdia, Apple still intends long-term adoption of OLED panels across MacBooks and iPads, but the transition pace has recently changed, owing to higher memory and component costs.

Previously, Omdia had expected Apple to discontinue its existing LCD-based models sooner, once its 14-inch and 16-inch OLED MacBook Pro models arrive – either this year or in early 2027.

However, Omdia now predicts that Apple will continue to sell both 14-inch and 16-inch LCD MacBook Pro models in parallel with the OLED MacBook Pro product line into at least 2028, a product strategy arrangement that is said to be based on cost factors.

Previous reports had already suggested Apple will position the OLED-based " MacBook Ultra " above the existing MacBook Pro models in its lineup, but there was little information about how long Apple would keep the latter models around for. Omdia's roadmap is the first to suggest they could remain available for another year at least.

articles.title: Apple Announces New M6 and M5 Pro Mac minis, Along with M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studios
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.

The headline feature of the M6 chip is that it’s Apple’s first 2-nanometer chip. The chip also includes “a larger 12-core CPU complex with the world’s fastest CPU core, a larger 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and up to 170GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.”

Looking more closely at the M6, Apple says it consists of two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores and is 1.2x faster in multithreaded performance than an M5 and up to 2.4x faster than an M1. Apple says the GPU delivers nearly 30% more peak GPU compute for AI than the M5. The M6’s 10% faster memory bandwidth will help with AI tasks, too, but its 32GB memory ceiling will limit which models can run locally.

The M6 mini’s GPU sounds impressive, too, with two more cores, Neural Accelerators for each core, which is a first for the mini. According to Apple, that leads to an up to four-fold increase in AI performance and a 2x graphics bump compared to the M4 mini. The Neural Engine has also been improved.

Apple also introduced an M5 Pro mini. It’s understandable if you find it confusing that the base model Mac mini has a more recent generation chipset than the more expensive model. What matters more than the chip generation is the “Pro” in M5 Pro, which makes it more capable than the M6, which has been designed for entry-level models.

The same sort of asymmetry occurred with the 2025 Mac Studio, which included an M4 Max model alongside the M3 Ultra. A big part of that difference is the M5 Pro mini’s support for 64GB of memory (double the M6 version’s top memory spec) and its 307GB/s of memory bandwidth compared to the M6 model’s 170GB/s memory bandwidth.

As for the M5 Ultra, which debuts in the Mac Studio, it sounds like a beast. According to Apple, the chip uses a next-generation version of its UltraFusion technology, resulting in a quad-die architecture for the first time in an Apple silicon chip. In addition, the M5 Ultra features an “up-to-36-core CPU and up-to-80-core GPU with a massive 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, 50 percent more than M3 Ultra.”

Here’s what Sri Santhanam, Apple’s vice president of Silicon Engineering Group, had to say about the new chips:

Today, we’re debuting the next giant leap in performance and AI compute for Apple silicon with the incredibly advanced M6 and the most powerful M-series chip yet, M5 Ultra. Built using the cutting-edge 2 nm process, M6 combines a new CPU complex, two additional CPU and GPU cores, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and more unified memory bandwidth to power through workloads with amazing energy efficiency.

And for the ultimate desktop performance and the ability to run massive AI models, M5 Ultra features a massive GPU, now with Neural Accelerators, and more unified memory bandwidth, pushing the boundaries of what a desktop can do.

Apple is fusing two dual-die M5 Max chips to create a single quad-die architecture. Apple says the M5 Ultra is “up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than M3 Ultra”, the fastest Mac previously for sale. The M5 Ultra also supports up to an 80-core GPU with up to 4.5x the peak GPU compute for AI tasks compared to the M3 Ultra and features an upgraded Media Engine, according to Apple.

For those who don’t need the bleeding-edge performance of the M5 Ultra, Apple also introduced what sounds like a very capable M5 Max Mac Studio. The M5 Max version of the computer “features an 18-core CPU, an up-to-40-core GPU with Neural Accelerators built into each core, and up to 128GB of unified memory, accelerating complex pro and AI workloads.”

Macs featuring the new chips won’t be available immediately. You can preorder both online today for delivery on September 22 with the caveat that the M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 512GB of memory won’t be available until later in October.

Prices have risen too. The Mac mini models are both $100 more than the models they replace, while the M5 Ultra Mac Studio’s base configuration has risen $200. However, the M5 Max Mac Studio’s starting price hasn’t changed.

The Mac mini has been a lot of things to a lot of people over the years. From a compact, minimalist desktop system to a headless server, the mini is Apple’s jack-of-all-trades. More recently, demand for the tiny computer has surged as people put them to work for a variety of AI tasks, including running LLMs locally and serving as standalone Hermes and OpenClaw machines.

With memory and storage constraints, it’s no surprise that the base prices of the mini have risen. Despite those challenges, I hope Apple is able to produce enough to meet demand. I’ve loved having an M4 Pro model working away day and night in the background. It’s fast, relatively cool, energy efficient, and easy to run remotely.

If the claims of Apple’s press release hold up under real-world use, I expect the new models will be the same, but faster and more capable, which is especially important for tasks like running models locally.

I’m also looking forward to seeing how the new Mac Studios perform in real world tests. I’ve used an M1 Max Mac Studio for a few years now and it’s been every bit the workhorse computer I need for my day-to-day work. However, it’s beginning to show its age when it comes to AI tasks, coding, and other tasks. It may finally be time for me to upgrade.

articles.subtitle: A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.
