articles.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker’s Final Boss Can Be Fought Immediately, but Will Destroy You
articles.subtitle: Two methods, both are brutally hard The Blood of Dawnwalker has a unique approach to structure, linearity, and player agency. The whole game is about trying to save your family from Brencis, the Knyaz of Vale Sangora, who has them held captive.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Two methods, both are brutally hard

The Blood of Dawnwalker has a unique approach to structure, linearity, and player agency. The whole game is about trying to save your family from Brencis, the Knyaz of Vale Sangora, who has them held captive. From the moment the prologue ends, you have up to 30 in-game days to make your way to Greifberg Castle, the most fortified building in the region, and take down the big bad Brencis once and for all.

Pre-launch, however, developer Rebel Wolves made it clear that if players want, they can make a beeline straight for the castle and attempt a rescue mission. I consider myself to be a competent video game player, and action RPGs are one of my most-played genres, so as soon as the prologue came to a close, I set a waypoint for the castle and started running.

The Blood of Dawnwalker's final boss will obliterate you

Folks, I cannot stress enough: I do not recommend you do this. I was doing it purely for science; of course I was going to reload my save and play the game at a normal pace afterward. But even getting to the castle is hell, because the further south you go, the stronger the enemies become. I had one hell of an entertaining dance with a huge green swamp worm before I could dash away to escape combat. Even the bog-standard wolves started to become a pain in my ass.

Eventually, I reached Svartrau, the only big city in Vale Sangora, and I navigated its streets toward the castle. I tell you what, dear reader: it was very amusing to see a pop-up warning me I was about to go past the point of no return when my playtime was just a couple of hours. Here we go, I thought; time to take down Brencis.

Unfortunately not. Turns out, as soon as you enter Greifberg Castle, a boss fight happens immediately, and it is not Brencis. Almost like a pre-boss boss fight, if you will. I won't spoil the dynamics of the fight, but let's just say that even on the easiest difficulty, using such low-level equipment means you need to have absolutely mastered The Blood of Dawnwalker's combat to even stand a chance. I managed to whittle down one of this boss's many health bar segments before I found myself impaled.

So running straight towards the boss isn't recommended. But it turns out there is a way to fight the very final boss even quicker, and bypass Greifberg Castle entirely. Thanks to my colleague, Johnny Wu, for finding this out: if you defeat Brencis during the prologue, shortly after you escape the mines, you will be taken straight to the very end of the game. No running across the whole map needed, nor do you have to win any pesky pre-boss boss fights.

No spoilers here for the final fight, but once again, I was quite obviously underprepared. It doesn't help that, because it takes place immediately after the prologue fight, you don't get a chance to heal. This means it's essentially one big boss fight, and the final boss is effectively the second stage. If anyone is able to beat the game in this way, huge kudos to you. I'm going back to playing the normal way... but you can unlock the game's secret ending right after the prologue too, if you like.

articles.title: A multi-month delay for Deus Ex turned into a huge payoff for one of its best characters, says designer Harvey Smith
articles.subtitle: Smith's story about the late stages of Deus Ex development takes some time to get to the point, but it's a fun ride.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Nobody likes game delays. Sure, a delay is temporary and suck is forever, as Gabe Newell once said, but it still chafes. But sometimes a little extra development time can go a very long way. In a new interview with the NoClip podcast, immersive sim maestro Harvey Smith shared one such story about Deus Ex, explaining how it leveraged some extra post-production time to give a much bigger role to one of the game's most famous NPCs—and make it a much better game in the process.

Smith's tale actually followed a remark by Ben Horne, his co-founder at the new Black Pony Immersive studio, who said, "You can elevate a good immersive sim into a great immersive sim in a very short amount of time, a matter of months, if you just protect a post-production time."

Publishers generally don't want to hear that, Smith added—although he obviously agrees with the sentiment—and so 20-some years ago, when Ion Storm Austin asked Eidos for more time to tighten up Deus Ex, "We geared up for this giant fight." Instead, Eidos just said yes.

"They were so distracted by what was happening in Dallas with Daikatana and such that they were like, 'Sure, sure, sure. Take five more months, take six more, whatever you need.' And we were like, 'Oh, cool. Okay'."

What was happening in Dallas, as Smith put it, was essentially chaos, which you can dig into via our history of Ion Storm. But, as Smith has previously related, it was a useful distraction for Ion Storm Austin, which did indeed get the extra time it wanted to really nail down Deus Ex.

A focus of that extra dev time was one of the game's foremost NPCs, "this German guy with a skull gun" named Gunther Hermann —who, for the record, very much wanted a skull gun but as far as I know never actually got one despite filing the required paperwork. "He's kind of a big presence in a couple of missions, you go on a mission with him, and then he just vanishes," Smith said. "He has no closure. He's not even in the game.

"So, I literally said, I can drop him into Paris, a big fight in the cathedral, which is an empty building right now, and I can hide some triggers on the roof with data links, and if you're crawling around on the roof because you have 'super jump' or whatever, I'll have him say, 'I'm watching you, Denton, like an insect crawl around on the roof.

I am watching you through the satellite, which I am linked to right now, Denton. ' You know, so we do this kind of thing, and players go, 'Well fuck, somebody's watching me from a satellite. ' It's like smoke and mirrors, and then you get in there and you fight it out with him.

"If you've been paying attention, you know that these earlier models, the cyborgs, they have kill phrases, him and Anna Navarre. And this was an idea that we took from Neil Stephenson or somewhere, so Denton can say this like long crazy kill phrase and Gunther just fucking dies, right? And it's a powerful moment. And we never would have had that in the game had we not gotten that extra time to just look at our game."

This is fascinating for me personally because I had that exact experience: Skulking around a Paris cathedral, quietly working my way inside, when all of a sudden Gunther busts in on the radio to let me know I'm not fooling anyone.

Giving it even more weight, I discovered before our final confrontation that Gunther had been waiting for me for some time—and that MJ12 troopers had heard him quietly crying, probably because I'd previously killed Navarre, his cyborg partner and someone for whom he apparently had deeper feelings than were immediately apparent.

Making it even better (and I swear this is true), Gunther bugged out near the end of our fight and ended up running into a corner of the cathedral basement, where he stood, silent and unmoving. He looked like what he was—an utterly beaten, broken man, who'd had everything taken away from him—and I couldn't bring myself to kill him.

At the time, I thought the option to show him mercy was intentional, like other hidden NPC choices in the game. (It didn't happen in subsequent playthroughs, though, and I've smoked ol' Gunther's ass every time since. )

It was a powerful moment, as Smith said, and it's kind of wild to imagine a version of Deus Ex where Gunther doesn't get his big finish—and what else might have been left on the cutting room floor besides. Something to keep in mind the next time you find yourself grinding your teeth over a delayed game.

Smith reiterated the importance of that point at the end of his story. "If you are listening to this right now and you fund games, give your team a post-production," he said. "Give them three to six extra months and you will win some awards and you will make a bunch of money, instead of leaving a crater in the ground."

articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple may introduce an entirely new 13.8-inch OLED MacBook model in 2029, potentially creating a new product tier between the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro, according to an updated product roadmap from research firm Omdia.

The firm's latest roadmap sandwiches a new 13.8-inch MacBook between the projected time line for the Air and Pro models. The surprise model is said to use a single-stack hybrid OLED panel, rather than the more sophisticated tandem OLED technology that is expected in the upcoming OLED MacBook Pro models, which are set to launch either later this year or early next year.

It seems this prediction hasn't come out of nowhere, either. According to a June report from ZDNet Korea, Apple sounded out Samsung Display, LG Display, and BOE for information regarding a 13.8-inch OLED MacBook panel earlier this year. At the time, the general assumption was that it was likely to be part of Apple's work on the first OLED MacBook Air, expected by 2028 at the earliest.

However, looking at Omdia's latest roadmap, the OLED MacBook Air is conspicuously absent, having been replaced by the 13.8-inch OLED machine in a separate "new" product category. The new model is expected to incorporate an LTPO+ backplane, integrated touch sensing, an under-panel camera, and a color filter integrated into the OLED encapsulation layer.

Omdia believes it is still too early to know for sure which display manufacturer would supply panels for the device, but the firm believes that it could potentially become an important mainstream MacBook product, positioned between the LCD MacBook Air and the higher-end OLED MacBook Pro.

Meanwhile, the MacBook Air line is shown as continuing to use LCD displays right into 2030.

articles.title: ChatGPT update adds Apple Messages integration on Mac
articles.subtitle: Well, this seems interesting. ChatGPT’s latest update adds a new Mac integration: the ability to work with conversations from Apple’s Messages app. The feature works with iMessage, SMS, and RCS.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Well, this seems interesting. ChatGPT’s latest update adds a new Mac integration: the ability to work with conversations from Apple’s Messages app. The feature works with iMessage, SMS, and RCS.

ChatGPT for Mac now includes an Apple Messages plugin

The new Apple Messages plugin lets ChatGPT read and search chats on a Mac, and prepare and send messages.

OpenAI says it is available across all plans in the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS, with support in both ChatGPT Work and Codex.

That access raises privacy and control questions, so OpenAI stresses that sending remains gated by user approval under the default settings.

Users should take care before granting persistent approval. OpenAI’s plugin guide details the risks and how to revoke access.

It also lists a known issue involving tasks that disable approval prompts: “If your task is set to Full access or otherwise disables approval prompts, Apple Messages may be unable to show the confirmation needed to send. Switch to Ask for approval or Approve for me and try again.”

How OpenAI’s Messages plugin works on the Mac

OpenAI explains that the optional Messages plugin runs locally on the Mac. Like other ChatGPT/Codex features including Computer Use, it relies on macOS system technologies like AppleScript and Accessibility.

The optional Messages plugin is not like the sketchy server-related hacks that try to bring iMessage functionality to Android. It’s simply using files on your Mac with your permission when prompted.

And unlike Siri AI, it doesn’t rely on an index of content from Messages. ChatGPT for Mac only uses the data when directed and with permission.

As you can see below, once enabled by the user, ChatGPT is super clear in what it does with messages, especially sending on your behalf when asked.

For these reasons, it shouldn’t be a privacy concern for Apple. The data exists as files on your Mac, and you need to give ChatGPT permission to work with the files. OpenAI also isn’t the only AI company to develop similar tools. It’s just a benefit of the Mac being a more capable operating system than mobile platforms.
